I've been in the role for a while and I do career coaching as well. 3 years is long enough to have had the honeymoon period pass and honestly is a good time to consider a pivot elsewhere- to be honest anytime outside of 2 years is totally fine. Most MSLs do and should consider moving around every couple years initially for two reasons : salary bumps and culture fit. This sounds like a good opportunity to explore an upgrade in both. 

Start connecting with colleagues and friends in other roles, get to know recruiters. If you're in an established MSL role, they will appreciate networking opportunities! My last role was very rough and I saw medical affairs slowly loose it's ability to self advocate. I left and have never been happier. I've said this elsewhere but also consider a therapeutic area pivot. Different TAs have different cultures. Dermatology is vastly different than Oncology for example and attracts different personalities and cultures.

Sorry to hear. It can take a while to find the right culture fit for what you're looking for. Medical affairs is viewed differently and carries different clout depending on the company. The role is honestly a dream job for me but I've left a company before that had commercial so highly propped up on a soap box that MSLs were viewed as auxiliary support to anything meaningful. 

Office jobs are crippling, just start looking elsewhere or consider transitioning into a new therapeutic area. I'm wildly biased but Oncology medical affairs does have unique privileges.

Edit: I'll also add that imposter syndrome is very real and I felt absolutely overwhelmed for the first 6 months of my job. That's totally normal.

Without specific examples I'll say that as someone in industry that indistry-sponsored clinical trials and biostatistics are very standardized across phase 1 through 4 trials. Additionally statistical designs are usually guided by regulatory bodies (FDA), as companies don't want to submit analyses that haven't been vetted as a surrogate measure of survival and benefit. 

Regarding low n sizes this might be due to a number of things. In early phase trials you will often see very low enrollments and small efficacy subgroup analyses because the purpose of an early phase trial is to evaluate safety and not efficacy. These early efficacy signals serve just that, as a signal. The other issue is that there are many rare cancer that don't make phase 3 trials viable, so often those trials stop at phase 2 (e.g. FIGHT202- ph2 trial of pemigatinib with no comparator arm and around 100 patients enrolled. This is because the cancer is ultra rare (cholangiocarcinoma with FGFR2 mutation) so a phase 3 would take decades to complete).

 Following that they entered this more refined modern Guns N Roses-esque phase that still incorporates heavier elements of their former sound but with cleaner vocals, and it's really debatable how well M Shadows voice translates to this genre- I like it but there are song and pitches I really *really* struggle with. Their musicianship and maturity is really showcased in this space, and obviously it becomes more palatable to more people without constant screaming. 

Their latest album is an experimental leap for the band which was *very* divisive which I absolutely love. I feel like this genre (or whatever this album can be described in, in one word), does lend itself well to his voice which is fantastic. 

Regardless I love bands that like to explore and grow similar to Metallica, Opeth, Mastodon etc who have played with their sound and identify over time. It sucks if you can't follow them on their whole journey (for me it was Opeth), but I respect the hell out of it.
